distinctions.title: fashionable vs trendy vs stylish
distinctions.text: *Fashionable* is neutral (popular now). *Trendy* is informal and can sound slightly critical. *Stylish* means attractive in a confident way, whether or not it is in fashion.

distinctions.title: historic vs historical
distinctions.text: *Historic* means important in history (*a historic victory*); *historical* means connected with the past (*historical documents*, *a historical novel*).

distinctions.title: critic vs criticism vs review
distinctions.text: A *critic* is a person; *criticism* is negative comment (or the activity of analysing art); a *review* is an article judging a book, film etc.

distinctions.title: economic vs economical
distinctions.text: *Economic* relates to the economy (*economic growth*). *Economical* means not wasting money or resources (*an economical car*).

distinctions.title: borrow vs lend vs loan
distinctions.text: You *borrow* money *from* someone; they *lend* it *to* you. *Loan* is the noun (and an informal verb in some varieties): *a bank loan*.

distinctions.title: city vs town vs village
distinctions.text: Size and status differ: a *village* is small and rural; a *town* is larger; a *city* is a large, important town (in the UK often one with a cathedral or royal charter).

distinctions.title: misinformation vs disinformation
distinctions.text: Both are false information. *Disinformation* is spread on purpose to deceive; *misinformation* may be spread by people who believe it.

distinctions.title: say vs tell vs speak vs talk
distinctions.text: *Tell* needs a person object (*tell me*); *say* doesn't (*say something*). *Speak* is more formal or about languages; *talk* suggests conversation.

distinctions.title: steal vs rob
distinctions.text: You *steal* a thing (*steal a phone*); you *rob* a person or place (*rob a bank*, *rob someone of something*).

distinctions.title: sentence vs verdict
distinctions.text: The *verdict* decides guilt (guilty / not guilty); the *sentence* is the punishment the judge gives afterwards.

distinctions.title: rise vs raise
distinctions.text: *Rise* is intransitive (*prices rose*); *raise* needs an object (*the bank raised interest rates*). Note the noun *a pay rise* (BrE) / *a raise* (AmE).

distinctions.title: fewer vs less
distinctions.text: In formal writing use *fewer* with countable nouns (*fewer jobs*) and *less* with uncountable nouns (*less money*).

distinctions.title: learn vs teach vs study
distinctions.text: You *learn* something (gain knowledge); someone *teaches* you; you *study* a subject (spend time learning it, often formally). ~~She learned me English~~ is wrong.

distinctions.title: university vs college vs school
distinctions.text: In British English *school* is for children (to 18); *college* often means further education or a part of a university; *university* awards degrees. In American English *school* and *college* can mean university.

distinctions.title: environmental vs environmentalist
distinctions.text: *Environmental* describes things connected with the natural world (*environmental damage*). An *environmentalist* is a person who works to protect it. Don't say ~~an environmental person~~.

distinctions.title: climate vs weather
distinctions.text: *Weather* is the conditions on a particular day; *climate* is the typical pattern over many years. *Climate change* is about long-term patterns, so ~~a hot climate today~~ is wrong.

distinctions.title: tasty vs tasteful
distinctions.text: *Tasty* means having a good flavour. *Tasteful* means attractive and showing good judgement in style (*a tasteful interior*), not food.

distinctions.title: cook vs cooker vs chef
distinctions.text: A *cook* or *chef* is a person (*chef* = professional). A *cooker* is a machine for cooking. ~~My mother is a good cooker~~ is wrong.

distinctions.title: disease vs illness vs injury
distinctions.text: A *disease* is a specific medical condition, often infectious (*heart disease*); *illness* is the state of being unwell; an *injury* is physical damage from an accident.

distinctions.title: cure vs treat vs heal
distinctions.text: You *treat* a patient or illness (try to make it better); you *cure* an illness (make it go away completely); wounds *heal*.

distinctions.title: antique vs ancient vs old-fashioned
distinctions.text: *Ancient* means extremely old, often thousands of years (*ancient Rome*). An *antique* is a valuable old object (furniture, jewellery). *Old-fashioned* means no longer modern or popular.

distinctions.title: funny vs fun
distinctions.text: *Fun* means enjoyable (*a fun evening*, *it was fun*). *Funny* means making you laugh, or strange (*a funny story*, *a funny smell*).

distinctions.title: uninhabited vs inhabited vs inhabitable
distinctions.text: *Inhabited* means people live there; *uninhabited* means nobody lives there; *uninhabitable* means people cannot live there. Note: *inhabitable* means the same as *habitable* (people can live there), not the opposite.

distinctions.title: wildlife vs nature
distinctions.text: *Nature* is the whole natural world; *wildlife* refers specifically to animals (and sometimes plants) living wild.

distinctions.title: sensible vs sensitive
distinctions.text: *Sensible* means having good judgement (*a sensible decision*). *Sensitive* means easily affected or aware of others' feelings (*a sensitive child*). Russian *сенситивный/чувствительный* = *sensitive*.

distinctions.title: nervous vs anxious vs apprehensive
distinctions.text: *Nervous* is everyday worry, often physical (*nervous before an exam*). *Anxious* is stronger or longer-lasting. *Apprehensive* is formal and about something in the future.

distinctions.title: sympathetic vs nice
distinctions.text: In English *sympathetic* means showing understanding of someone's problems, NOT attractive or pleasant. Russian *симпатичный* is *nice*, *likeable* or *attractive*.

distinctions.title: alone vs lonely
distinctions.text: *Alone* means without other people (neutral). *Lonely* means unhappy because you are alone or have no friends.

distinctions.title: chance vs opportunity vs possibility
distinctions.text: *Possibility* is something that might happen. *Chance* is likelihood (*a good chance of rain*) or luck. An *opportunity* is a favourable moment to do something (*a job opportunity*).

distinctions.title: invention vs discovery
distinctions.text: You *discover* something that already existed (a planet, a law of nature); you *invent* something new that did not exist before (a machine, a process).

distinctions.title: technique vs technology
distinctions.text: A *technique* is a way of doing something (a surgical technique); *technology* is the machines and scientific knowledge used to do it.

distinctions.title: politics vs policy vs politician
distinctions.text: *Politics* is the activity of government and power (*interested in politics*). A *policy* is a particular plan (*a new transport policy*). A *politician* is a person in politics.

distinctions.title: affect vs effect
distinctions.text: *Affect* is usually a verb (*the cuts affect the poor*); *effect* is usually a noun (*the effect of the cuts*). *Effect* as a verb means *bring about* (*effect change*).

distinctions.title: play vs do vs go
distinctions.text: Use *play* with ball games and competitive games (*play tennis*), *go* with activities ending in -ing (*go swimming*), and *do* with other activities, especially individual ones (*do yoga*, *do judo*).

distinctions.title: beat vs win
distinctions.text: You *win* a game, match or prize; you *beat* an opponent. ~~We won them~~ is wrong.

distinctions.title: emigrate vs immigrate vs migrate
distinctions.text: You *emigrate from* your country and *immigrate to* a new one. *Migrate* is the general word, also used for animals and seasonal moves.

distinctions.title: travel vs trip vs journey
distinctions.text: *Travel* (uncountable) is the general activity. A *journey* is going from one place to another (*a long train journey*). A *trip* includes going, staying and returning (*a business trip*). ~~a travel~~ is wrong.

distinctions.title: job vs work vs career
distinctions.text: *Work* is uncountable and general (*I have a lot of work*). A *job* is countable: a particular paid position (*She got a new job*). A *career* is the series of jobs in one field across your working life.

distinctions.title: sack vs lay off
distinctions.text: You are *sacked* (*fired*) because of something you did wrong; you are *laid off* (*made redundant*) because the employer no longer needs your role.
